Identify the categories of employers and employees covered by the mandatory group life insurance obligation.
Define 'annual total emolument' and calculate the minimum sum assured for employees at different salary levels.
Explain the nature and legal effect of the master policy and the certificate of participation.
Describe the underwriting principles specific to group life insurance, including the free cover limit, automatic acceptance, and the treatment of late entrants.
Explain how premiums for group life schemes are calculated, including the rate-per-thousand and the claims experience adjustment.
Describe the scheme administration process: additions, deletions, mid-year changes, and renewal procedures.

Explain the claims process for group life schemes, including the documentation required, the removal of the Letters of Administration requirement under PRA 2014, and NIIRA 2025's claims settlement obligations.

blocks.text: 7.1  Introduction: The Group Concept in Life Insurance

blocks.h: Life insurance sold to individuals requires a proposal, an underwriting assessment, a medical examination (above certain sum thresholds), a policy document, and a premium calculated on the specific mortality risk of that individual. Group life insurance proceeds on an entirely different logic: instead of insuring individual lives one by one, it insures a defined group of people under a single master contract, treating the group as a single actuarial unit whose aggregate mortality experience can be predicted and priced without individual medical assessment of most members.

This structural difference — from individual to collective risk assessment — produces three major commercial advantages. First, economies of scale: one contract, one premium calculation, one administration structure for potentially thousands of lives. Second, cost efficiency: the group rate per unit of cover is typically significantly lower than the individual rate, because the insurer's expense loading is spread across many lives. Third, accessibility: group membership provides life cover to individuals who might not otherwise seek or qualify for individual life assurance — particularly in Nigeria, where mass-market individual life insurance penetration is extremely low.

Group life insurance is the most widely held form of life insurance in Nigeria. The reason is legislative, not market-driven: the Pension Reform Act 2014, building on the original Pension Reform Act 2004, mandates every employer in Nigeria with three or more employees to maintain a Group Life Insurance Policy for all employees. This mandate has made group life insurance the single largest source of premium volume and of insured lives in the Nigerian life insurance market. Understanding it fully — its legal basis, its mechanics, its administration, and its claims process — is therefore not merely academically important; it is practically indispensable.
The foundational legal instrument governing employer-sponsored group life insurance in Nigeria is the Pension Reform Act 2014 (PRA 2014). Section 4(5) of the Act provides in full:<sup>[1]</sup>

"Every employer shall maintain a Group Life Insurance Policy in favour of each employee for a minimum of three times the annual total emolument of the employee and premium shall be paid not later than the date of commencement of the cover."

This provision establishes three non-negotiable obligations: the obligation to maintain cover (not merely to purchase it once but to maintain it continuously in force), the minimum benefit threshold (three times annual total emolument), and the payment timing (premium must be paid before cover commences — preserving the 'no premium, no cover' principle in the group context).
Section 4(6) of the PRA 2014 addresses what happens when an employer fails to maintain cover:<sup>[2]</sup>

"Where the employer failed, refused or omitted to make payment as and when due, the employer shall make arrangement to pay the equivalent of the death benefit, disability benefit or both, as may be applicable to the insurer for the benefit of any deceased or disabled employee."

The significance of this provision cannot be overstated: a non-compliant employer does not merely face a regulatory fine. They become directly liable to pay the death benefit out of their own funds to the estate of any employee who dies while the mandatory cover was not in place. Given that the minimum benefit is three times annual emolument — potentially several million naira for a senior employee — this is an existential financial risk for an under-resourced employer. Understanding this liability is the most powerful compliance argument available to an adviser selling group life to a reluctant employer.

blocks.title: Regulatory Spotlight — PRA 2014 and NIIRA 2025 — The Group Life Mandate: Summary of Obligations

blocks.h: Every employer in Nigeria with three or more employees is subject to the following obligations:

items.h: Maintain a Group Life Insurance Policy: The policy must be issued by a NAICOM-licensed life insurer authorised to write group life assurance business. A group life certificate from an unlicensed entity does not satisfy the legal obligation.

Minimum benefit: Three times the annual total emolument (ATE) of each employee. ATE = Annual Basic Salary + Annual Housing Allowance + Annual Transportation Allowance. Some employers use Gross Annual Salary as the ATE, which NAICOM and PenCom permit where it is more generous.
Premium payment timing: Premium must be paid in full before the commencement of cover. Partial premium payment does not create a valid insurance contract under Nigerian law.

Annual renewal: The Group Life Insurance Certificate, once obtained, must be renewed annually. The renewed certificate must be submitted to the National Pension Commission (PenCom) as evidence of compliance.

Employer bears the full cost: The mandatory group life scheme is non-contributory — the employer pays the entire premium. Voluntary supplementary cover above the mandatory minimum may be contributory (employee-funded or co-funded), but the mandatory minimum must be fully employer-funded.

Penalty for non-compliance: Under NIIRA 2025, employers who fail to maintain the mandatory group life policy face a fine of ₦250,000 per uninsured employee. Additionally, under PRA 2014 Section 4(6), the employer bears direct financial liability for any death benefit that would have been payable had the policy been in place.

blocks.h: Sources: PRA 2014, Sections 4(5) and 4(6); PenCom Revised Guidelines on Group Life Insurance Policy (2020); NIIRA 2025, compulsory insurance provisions.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

blocks.text: 7.2.2  The Employee Threshold: Three or More

blocks.h: The Pension Reform Act 2014 reduced the employee threshold for the mandatory group life obligation from the five employees required under the original Pension Reform Act 2004 to three employees. This change substantially expanded the universe of covered employers and employees, particularly affecting the micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME) sector which constitutes the backbone of Nigerian private employment.<sup>[6]</sup>

The practical implication is that virtually every formally registered employer in Nigeria — from a three-person consultancy to a major conglomerate — is legally obligated to maintain group life insurance. The major exception is sole traders without employees and wholly informal businesses, which operate outside the formal employment framework the PRA 2014 addresses. As formalisation of the Nigerian economy progresses and more businesses register with the CAC, the universe of legally compelled group life purchasers expands.

blocks.text: 7.2.3  PenCom's Revised Guidelines on Group Life Insurance (2020)

blocks.h: The Revised Guidelines on Group Life Insurance Policy for Employees (2020), issued jointly by the National Pension Commission (PenCom) and NAICOM, provide the detailed operational rules for administering the mandatory group life scheme. These guidelines clarify: the definition of annual total emolument; the eligibility criteria for covered employees; the procedure for submitting the Group Life Insurance Certificate to PenCom; and the obligations of insurers, employers, and brokers in the administration of the scheme. The guidelines apply alongside NIIRA 2025 and are the primary operational reference for practitioners administering group life schemes in Nigeria.<sup>[4]</sup>

blocks.text: 7.3  The Structure of a Group Life Scheme: Parties and Documents

blocks.h: The master policy is the single insurance contract issued by the insurer to the employer (the policyholder). It is the legal document establishing the terms of the group life scheme: the benefit levels, the premium rates, the eligibility rules, the definitions of covered events (death, total and permanent disability), the exclusions, the claims process, and the scheme administration requirements. The master policy is held by the employer; individual employees receive certificates of participation, not copies of the master policy.

The single insurance contract issued by the insurer to the employer (the group policyholder), establishing the terms of the group life scheme. The master policy governs the rights and obligations of the insurer and the employer. Individual employees are covered under the scheme by virtue of their membership of the group, not through individual contractual relationships with the insurer. The master policy is the definitive document for claims assessment and scheme administration.
Cf: Certificate of participation — the document issued to each individual employee evidencing their membership of the group scheme and the benefit to which they are entitled.

Each employee covered under the group life scheme receives a certificate of participation — a document confirming their coverage under the master policy. The certificate states the employee's name, the scheme name, the sum assured applicable to that employee (based on their annual total emolument), the benefit multiplier, the effective date of cover, the name of the insurer, and the claims notification procedure.

The certificate is not a separate contract — it is evidence of membership of the group scheme. The terms and conditions governing the employee's cover are those of the master policy; the certificate merely confirms the individual's participation. This means that changes to the master policy terms — at renewal, for example — affect all employees whether or not they have been individually notified, provided the employer has accepted the revised terms.

blocks.text: 7.4  Annual Total Emolument: Definition and Calculation

blocks.h: The term 'annual total emolument' (ATE) is the benchmark for calculating the mandatory minimum sum assured under the PRA 2014 and the group life scheme. It is defined in Nigerian practice and confirmed by PenCom's guidelines as comprising the following components of an employee's annual gross compensation:<sup>[7]</sup>

items.h: Annual Basic Salary: The fixed base salary component, excluding all allowances and variable pay.
Annual Housing Allowance: Any fixed housing allowance provided as part of the compensation package.
Annual Transportation Allowance: Any fixed transport allowance provided as part of the compensation package.

blocks.h: The ATE calculation therefore includes the core salary components but excludes purely performance-based pay such as commissions, bonuses, and overtime. Some employers define ATE as total gross salary — which may produce a higher ATE than the statutory minimum definition — and this is permitted where it is more generous to the employee. The key regulatory requirement is that the ATE used must produce a sum assured of at least three times the statutory ATE; using a lower base (for example, basic salary only without housing and transport) to reduce the sum assured is non-compliant.

blocks.title: Illustration — Annual Total Emolument Calculation — Three Employee Examples

blocks.h: Key observations: (1) The minimum benefit for even a junior employee is ₦6.12 million — a sum that most Nigerian families would find life-changing. (2) The employer bears the full annual premium, which at typical group life rates (0.15–0.25% of sum assured) is modest relative to the protection provided. (3) For a company with 50 employees averaging ₦5.4 million ATE each, the total annual group life premium would be approximately ₦1.6 million — less than the monthly salary of a mid-level manager.

blocks.text: 7.4.2  The Benefit Multiplier: Minimum and Market Practice

blocks.h: The law mandates a minimum multiplier of three times ATE. In practice, many Nigerian employers, particularly in the financial services, oil and gas, and technology sectors, offer more generous group life multiples as part of their employee benefits strategy:

items.h: 3× ATE: The statutory minimum. Compliant. Used primarily by SMEs operating with tight employment cost budgets.
4× ATE: A common 'slightly above minimum' practice used by mid-tier employers seeking to demonstrate employee welfare commitment beyond bare compliance.
5× ATE: Common in the financial services sector and among multinational companies operating in Nigeria.
6× ATE and above: Typical of the largest employers — major banks, international oil companies, leading technology firms — for whom group life is a competitive employee benefits differentiator.

blocks.h: The additional cost of moving from 3× to 5× ATE is proportionally modest — approximately 66% more premium — while providing employees with a 66% larger death benefit. Advisers and HR managers should present this cost-benefit comparison to employers who default to the statutory minimum without considering the reputational and talent retention benefits of more generous cover.

Individual life underwriting assesses each applicant's personal risk profile — age, health, occupation, lifestyle — and prices accordingly. Group underwriting takes an entirely different approach: it assesses the risk characteristics of the group as a whole, treating the group's aggregate mortality experience as the pricing basis rather than any individual member's profile. This group approach is justified by the law of large numbers: provided the group is large enough and sufficiently homogeneous, the expected mortality experience is predictable without individual assessment.

The practical consequence is that most members of a group life scheme join without any medical examination, health questionnaire, or individual underwriting assessment. This is the primary accessibility advantage of group insurance: it opens life cover to individuals who might have difficulty obtaining individual cover due to health conditions, occupational hazards, or financial barriers to a full individual application process.

The assessment of the mortality risk of a defined group as a single actuarial unit, rather than as a collection of individually assessed lives. Group underwriting is less stringent than individual underwriting: most group members are accepted automatically (without medical evidence) up to the Free Cover Limit. Above the FCL, individual medical evidence is required. The group rate (premium per ₦1,000 of sum assured) is calculated based on the group's age profile, industry hazard classification, size, and — for renewals — actual claims experience.

Key principle: The group must be formed for a purpose other than insurance. A group assembled solely to obtain insurance at group rates — a 'contrived group' — does not qualify for group underwriting terms.

The Free Cover Limit (FCL) is the maximum sum assured per individual employee at which the insurer will accept that employee into the group scheme automatically, without requiring individual medical evidence. Below the FCL, all employees in an eligible category (based on age and employment status) are automatically covered. Above the FCL, the insurer requires the employee to provide a satisfactory medical declaration, attend a medical examination, or both before cover at the higher amount takes effect.

The FCL is agreed between the insurer and the employer at scheme inception and is influenced by the size of the group, the average age of members, the industry's occupational hazard profile, and the insurer's risk appetite. For a scheme of 50 employees with an average age of 38, the FCL might be set at ₦20 million or equivalent — meaning all employees whose sum assured is below ₦20 million are auto-accepted. A senior manager whose sum assured (5× ATE) is ₦40 million would need to submit evidence of good health for the excess ₦20 million above the FCL.

The maximum amount of life cover per individual employee that an insurer will grant under a group scheme without requiring individual medical evidence. All eligible employees whose sum assured falls at or below the FCL are automatically accepted. Those whose sum assured exceeds the FCL must provide satisfactory individual medical evidence for the excess. The FCL is scheme-specific and is set by the insurer at inception based on group size, age profile, and risk classification.
Note: The FCL is sometimes called the 'Non-Medical Limit' (NML) in group underwriting. It is not the same as the non-medical limit in individual underwriting, which is a fixed market-wide threshold.
To be covered under a group life scheme, an employee must satisfy eligibility conditions as specified in the master policy. Standard eligibility requirements in the Nigerian market include:

items.h: Employment status: Only permanent (full-time) employees are automatically eligible. Contract staff, casual workers, and independent contractors may be included at the employer's option, but their inclusion must be specified in the master policy and may carry a premium loading.

Age at entry: Typically 18 to 60 years (extendable to 65 for Professors and Judges under PenCom's special provisions). An employee who enters the scheme above the maximum entry age is excluded from cover.

Actively at work: Many master policies require the employee to be 'actively at work' on the effective date of their cover — meaning not on sick leave, hospitalised, or on extended disability leave. An employee who is not actively at work on the effective date has their cover deferred until they return to active work.

Waiting period: Some schemes impose a short waiting period (commonly 3 months) before a new entrant's cover takes effect, to prevent adverse selection through the immediate hiring of terminally ill individuals.

blocks.h: Late entrants — employees who join the scheme after its inception date — are typically subject to a short waiting period and may need to provide a health declaration if they are joining after the initial free entry period. This prevents an employer from 'adding' a critically ill employee to the scheme shortly before death, specifically to generate a claim.<sup>[16]</sup>

blocks.text: 7.5.4  The Group Rate and Premium Calculation

blocks.h: The group life premium is calculated as a rate per ₦1,000 of total sum assured across all covered members. The insurer determines the rate based on:

items.h: Age profile of the group: The weighted average age (or the age distribution) is the primary mortality driver. An older workforce has a higher mortality rate and attracts a higher rate per ₦1,000.

Industry classification: Some industries carry higher occupational hazard risks — oil and gas, construction, manufacturing, mining — and attract loadings above the standard rate. Office-based professional services attract the base rate.
Group size: Larger groups achieve better rates due to actuarial credibility and lower per-unit administrative cost. A scheme of 500 employees will achieve a better rate than a scheme of 20.

Claims experience (for renewals): At renewal, the insurer reviews the scheme's actual claims experience during the year. A scheme with more deaths than expected (adverse experience) will see its rate increase; one with fewer deaths (favourable experience) may receive a rate reduction or retention credit.

blocks.title: Illustration — Group Life Premium Calculation — Worked Example

blocks.h: A Lagos-based technology company has 120 employees covered under a group life scheme. The total sum assured across all members (at the agreed 4× ATE benefit level) is ₦3,840,000,000 (₦3.84 billion). The insurer quotes a standard group life rate of ₦0.20 per ₦1,000 of sum assured.

Per-employee cost analysis: ₦768,000 ÷ 120 employees = ₦6,400 per employee per year. This translates to a monthly cost of approximately ₦533 per employee for protection averaging ₦32 million per life — one of the most cost-effective financial safety nets available in any market.

blocks.text: 7.6  Scheme Administration: Additions, Deletions, and Renewals

blocks.h: The employer is the scheme administrator in the day-to-day operational sense: it is the employer's HR and finance departments that maintain the employee census, notify the insurer of changes, and pay the premiums. Effective scheme administration is critical to ensuring that cover is current, accurate, and enforceable when a claim arises. A claim that is denied because the deceased employee was not on the current insured schedule is a compliance failure with potentially serious legal and reputational consequences for the employer.

The employee schedule (or scheme schedule) is the list of covered employees maintained by the insurer under the master policy. It records each employee's name, date of birth, annual total emolument, applicable sum assured, date of cover commencement, and beneficiary designation. The schedule is the definitive record of who is covered and for how much; a claim can only be processed for an employee who appears on the current schedule with an active status.

The employer must update the schedule promptly whenever changes occur: new hires, terminations, salary adjustments (which change the sum assured), promotions, and deaths. Most insurers provide a web portal or a structured Excel template for schedule maintenance; some have integrated with payroll systems to automate schedule updates. The trend in the Nigerian market — driven by Insurtech adoption — is towards API-connected group life administration platforms that synchronise employee data between the employer's HR system and the insurer's policy administration system in real time.

When a new employee joins the company, the employer must notify the insurer and add the employee to the scheme schedule within the period specified in the master policy (typically 30 days of employment commencement). Cover commences from the date of employment or from the date of notification to the insurer, whichever is later, subject to the actively-at-work condition and any applicable waiting period.

The additional premium for new joiners is calculated on a pro-rata basis: if an employee joins six months into the annual scheme period, the additional premium due is half the annual premium for that employee. The employer settles the pro-rata addition with each quarter's renewal or as a separate endorsement to the master policy.

When an employee leaves the company — through resignation, redundancy, retirement, or termination — their cover under the group scheme automatically ceases on the last day of employment. The employer must notify the insurer of the deletion and the insurer adjusts the premium for the next period accordingly (credit for the remaining period of the leaver's cover, which is typically carried forward to offset the cost of new joiners).

It is essential that the employer processes deletions promptly. An employee who has left the company but remains on the insured schedule creates a premium overcharge (the employer is paying for someone who is no longer employed) and a potential claims risk (if the former employee dies, a spurious claim might be submitted on the basis of an outdated schedule). NAICOM's market conduct standards require insurers to ensure that their schedule records are current and verified at each renewal.

blocks.text: 7.6.4  Salary Reviews and Sum Assured Adjustments

blocks.h: When an employer conducts an annual salary review and increases employees' salaries, the ATE of covered employees increases, and therefore the minimum sum assured under the mandatory scheme also increases. The employer must notify the insurer of salary changes and adjust the scheme accordingly. Failure to update the sum assured to reflect current ATE means the scheme is providing a benefit below the statutory minimum — a compliance breach and a shortfall in cover for affected employees' families.

Most group life master policies provide an automatic sum assured adjustment mechanism: at each annual renewal, the insurer adjusts all sums assured based on the updated salary schedule submitted by the employer. The revised premium for the new policy year reflects the updated benefit levels. Employers should build this schedule update into their annual compensation review calendar.

blocks.title: Process — Group Life Scheme — Annual Renewal Process

blocks.h: The group life scheme is typically renewed annually. The renewal process follows these stages:

items.h: 90 days before expiry: The broker (or employer's HR team) initiates the renewal. The current employee schedule is reviewed and updated — new hires added, leavers removed, salary changes reflected.

60 days before expiry: The updated schedule is submitted to the insurer. The insurer reviews the claims experience of the expiring year, assesses any changes in group composition or risk profile, and prepares a renewal quotation.

45 days before expiry: The renewal premium is calculated and quoted. The broker negotiates on behalf of the employer, particularly where the claims experience has been favourable or where the group has grown. Market testing (obtaining competitive quotations from alternative insurers) is common for larger schemes.

30 days before expiry: Premium payment is made in full to the insurer. NIIRA 2025 and PRA 2014 both require premium payment before commencement of cover — a late payment creates a gap in coverage. The renewed Group Life Insurance Certificate is issued by the insurer.

Before expiry: The renewed certificate is submitted by the employer to PenCom as annual evidence of compliance with the PRA 2014 group life obligation. Submission to PenCom is a critical compliance step — the absence of a current certificate in PenCom's records triggers a compliance query and potential sanctions.
Continuous: The broker or employer updates the insured schedule throughout the year as the workforce changes, maintaining the accuracy of cover at all times.

blocks.h: Note: A gap in cover — even one day between the expiry of the old policy and the commencement of the new — means no insurer is on risk for deaths occurring in that gap. The employer bears direct financial liability for such deaths under PRA 2014, Section 4(6). Timely renewal is therefore both a regulatory requirement and a financial imperative.[12]

blocks.text: 7.7  Premium Financing: Contributory vs Non-Contributory Schemes

blocks.h: The PRA 2014's mandatory group life obligation is expressly non-contributory: the employer bears the full annual premium with no contribution required from employees. This is confirmed in PenCom's Revised Guidelines. However, many employers choose to operate a dual-layer scheme: the mandatory non-contributory base layer (funded entirely by the employer at the statutory minimum of 3× ATE) and an optional supplementary layer (which employees may elect to purchase at their own cost, providing additional cover above the minimum).<sup>[9]</sup>

blocks.title: Advisory — Contributory Scheme Design — Advisory for HR Managers and Benefits Consultants

blocks.h: When designing a contributory supplementary layer above the mandatory non-contributory base, advisers and HR managers should consider the following best practices:

items.h: Multiple benefit options: Offer employees a choice of benefit levels (e.g. 4×, 5×, 6×, or 8× ATE) rather than a single level. This allows employees to self-select based on their personal financial circumstances and family obligations.

Tax implications: Group life premium paid by the employer is a deductible business expense. Employee contributions under a supplementary scheme may also be structured to obtain tax efficiency — consult a tax adviser on the current treatment under the Personal Income Tax Act.

Enrolment and changes: Establish clear annual enrolment periods during which employees may join, upgrade, or downgrade their supplementary cover. Changes outside the enrolment period should require evidence of insurability to prevent adverse selection.

Communication: Employees who do not understand the value of their group life cover are not retaining it as a benefit. Annual benefits communication — including a personalised benefit statement showing each employee their current sum assured in naira — significantly increases appreciation of the employer's investment in their welfare.

blocks.text: 7.8  Claims under a Group Life Scheme

blocks.h: A group life death claim arises when a covered employee dies while in active service and while the master policy is in force. The claims process is managed primarily by the employer, who interfaces with the insurer (directly or through the broker) to gather and submit the required documentation. Unlike individual life assurance claims — where the policyholder and the claimant may be the same person — group life claims involve the employer (as policyholder), the insurer, and the deceased employee's nominated beneficiary as three distinct parties.

blocks.title: Process — Group Life Death Claim — Documentation and Process

blocks.h: The following documents are typically required to process a group life death claim in Nigeria:

items.h: Notification: Written notification of the employee's death to the insurer (or broker) as soon as practicable after the death. The master policy specifies the notification period — typically 30 days.
Completed claim form: The insurer's standard group life claim form, completed by the employer.
Death certificate: A certified copy of the employee's death certificate, issued by the Nigerian Civil Registration Authority or equivalent.
Employee record: Confirmation from the employer of the employee's name, date of birth, employment commencement date, position, annual total emolument, and sum assured at the date of death.
Beneficiary identification: Proof of identity of the named beneficiary (government-issued ID), and the beneficiary's bank account details for payment.
Scheme schedule confirmation: Confirmation that the deceased employee was on the active insured schedule at the date of death.

No Letter of Administration required: Under Section 8(1) of the PRA 2014, the death benefit under a group life policy is paid directly to the named beneficiary without requiring a Court order (Letters of Administration or Probate). This is a critical reform that accelerates claims settlement for beneficiaries.

blocks.h: Where no beneficiary has been nominated by the deceased employee, the benefit is paid to the next of kin as determined by the employer's records and in accordance with Nigerian succession laws. NAICOM's market conduct guidance encourages employers to collect and maintain current beneficiary nomination forms from all covered employees as part of routine HR administration. An outdated or missing beneficiary designation is a significant claims complication.<sup>[3]</sup>

Under NIIRA 2025, all insurance claims — including group life death claims — must be settled within 60 days of notification of the claim, or such shorter period as NAICOM may specify in implementing regulations. An insurer that fails to settle a valid claim within this period is liable to pay compound interest on the outstanding claim amount for every month of delay. The insurer must, within the settlement period, either pay the claim or provide written notification of the grounds for dispute.<sup>[18]</sup>

The NIIRA 2025 claims timeline requirement is particularly significant for group life beneficiaries, who are often widows, orphans, or elderly parents dependent on the death benefit for immediate financial survival. Pre-NIIRA 2025, group life claims were often delayed for months or even years — particularly on the Federal Government's own scheme, which became notorious for unpaid benefits. The compound interest penalty is designed to make delay financially irrational for insurers; combined with NAICOM's enforcement mandate, it creates a structural incentive for prompt settlement.

Group life claims may be contested where: (a) the insurer disputes that the employee was on the active schedule at the time of death; (b) the insurer alleges that the death occurred outside the cover period (e.g. during a gap in cover due to late premium payment); (c) an exclusion clause applies (suicide, for example, is typically excluded under most group life policies during an initial period); or (d) there is suspicion of fraudulent documentation.

Fraudulent group life claims are a recognised problem in the Nigerian market. Common fraud patterns include: fabricating a death when the employee has actually emigrated or gone into hiding; manipulating the employee schedule retrospectively to include a terminally ill or recently deceased person; and submitting claims for fictitious employees. NAICOM requires insurers to maintain anti-fraud protocols for group life claims, including verification of death certificates with the National Population Commission and cross-checking claim submissions against payroll records provided by the employer.

The mandatory group life scheme covers death only — it is, at its core, a group term assurance on all covered employees' lives. Many employers choose to enhance the scheme with optional additional benefits that provide broader employee welfare protection. These optional enhancements are subject to NAICOM product approval and actuarial pricing, and their cost is determined by the specific benefit structure agreed.<sup>[13]</sup>

rows: Pays specified benefits (death, total/permanent disability, temporary total disability, medical expenses) for injuries arising from accidents. The most common group life enhancement in Nigeria — covers the high-risk of road traffic accidents, offshore work incidents, and industrial injuries.

Pays the sum assured (or a proportion thereof) if an employee becomes totally and permanently disabled and unable to work. Typically structured as equivalent to the death benefit or a specified fraction of it.
For contributory supplementary schemes, the employee's contributions are waived if they become disabled. Less common in Nigeria but growing in corporate benefit packages.

Pays a fixed lump sum (typically ₦50,000–₦250,000) towards funeral and burial costs on an employee's death. A practical and highly valued addition in the Nigerian context where burial costs can be substantial.
Pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a specified serious illness. Relatively new in Nigerian group schemes but growing in the financial services sector where employee health is a productivity concern.
Extends the group death benefit to cover the employee's spouse and/or dependent children. Typically at a lower multiple (e.g. 1× spouse's income or a fixed sum per dependent).

blocks.text: 7.10  Portability and Conversion on Termination of Employment

blocks.h: A fundamental limitation of group life insurance is that cover is tied to employment: when an employee leaves the company, their group life cover ceases immediately and automatically. For a senior employee who has enjoyed substantial group life cover for many years — and who may now be older or have developed health conditions that make fresh individual underwriting difficult — losing group cover at termination can create a significant protection gap.

Two mechanisms are available in international and increasingly in Nigerian group life practice to address this gap: portability and conversion. Both options must be explicitly provided for in the master policy; they are not automatic rights under NIIRA 2025 or the PRA 2014 as currently implemented. Practitioners advising on group scheme design should advocate for their inclusion.

Portability (sometimes called 'porting') allows a departing employee to convert their group life coverage into a new term life insurance policy with the same insurer, continuing cover for an agreed period without a gap and without fresh individual underwriting. The premium on the ported policy is re-calculated at the employee's attained age at the time of departure and reflects individual (rather than group) rates — it will therefore typically be higher than the group rate — but the key advantage is that no new medical evidence is required.<sup>[17]</sup>

Portability is exercised within a strict window — typically 30 to 60 days after the group cover termination date. An employee who misses this window loses the portability right and must apply for fresh individual cover, subject to full underwriting. Employers have a fiduciary duty to notify departing employees of their portability right and to provide the necessary forms within a reasonable time of employment termination.

Conversion is a more comprehensive option: it allows the departing employee to convert their group term life cover to an individual permanent (typically whole life) policy with the same insurer, without providing evidence of insurability. The conversion right applies regardless of the employee's health status — even an employee diagnosed with a terminal illness can convert their group term cover to a permanent individual policy, provided the conversion is exercised within the prescribed window.

Conversion rights are more favourable to the employee than portability rights but are also more costly for the insurer — the insurer cannot re-underwrite the converted life. The conversion premium is set at the insurer's standard individual rate for the employee's age at conversion, regardless of health status. This pooling of potentially adverse lives is the price the insurer pays for offering conversion rights, and it is reflected in the group scheme's pricing (a small loading for the conversion option).

Rights that may be attached to a group life master policy allowing departing employees to continue life insurance cover on an individual basis without fresh underwriting. Portability: the employee continues term cover with the same insurer, premium at attained age, no medical evidence required if exercised within the prescribed window. Conversion: the employee converts term cover to a permanent individual policy (typically whole life), premium at attained age without health assessment, regardless of current health status. Both rights expire if not exercised within the prescribed window (typically 30–60 days after group cover termination).

Advisory: Employers should ensure that all termination documentation (resignation letters, redundancy notices, retirement notifications) include written notice of portability and conversion rights and the applicable exercise deadline.

blocks.text: 7.11  Market Conduct, Rate Competition, and the 9% Commission Cap

blocks.h: The group life assurance market in Nigeria has historically been characterised by intense and sometimes destructive rate competition — particularly on the Federal Government's own group life scheme, which became a focal point for premium undercutting in the early 2000s. Insurers, competing for the premium volume of the Federal Government scheme (which covered hundreds of thousands of civil servants), were found to be quoting rates so low that the mathematical adequacy of the premium was questionable. This created a situation where the insurer's obligation to pay death benefits substantially exceeded the premium collected — a recipe for insolvency and unpaid claims.<sup>[10]</sup>

NAICOM's response was to impose a cap on group life commission (8% in its 2011 Operational Guidelines), limiting the proportion of the premium that could be paid as intermediary commission. This reduced the intermediary's incentive to recommend the lowest-priced insurer (since the commission was now a fixed percentage rather than the entirety of whatever margin remained after the premium was paid to the insurer). NIIRA 2025 s.62(1)(a) now fixes the statutory maximum for group life at 9% of the premium.

For practitioners, the lesson from the Federal Government scheme controversy is clear: selecting the lowest premium is not always in the client's interest. An insurer offering a rate that is materially below the actuarial expectation for the scheme's risk profile is either cross-subsidising from other business, underestimating the claims risk, or planning to decline claims on technical grounds. The CIIN Code of Ethics and NAICOM's market conduct requirements impose on brokers and advisers an obligation to consider not merely price but financial strength, claims settlement record, and regulatory compliance status when recommending an insurer for a group life scheme.

blocks.title: Advisory — Selecting a Group Life Insurer — Due Diligence Checklist

blocks.h: When advising an employer client on insurer selection for their group life scheme, practitioners should apply the following due diligence framework:

items.h: NAICOM licence verification: Confirm the insurer holds a current life insurance licence with authority to write group life business. Check naicom.gov.ng's public register.

Capital adequacy: Verify the insurer is in compliance with NIIRA 2025's capital requirements (minimum ₦10 billion for life insurers). Insurers below the new threshold are in the recapitalisation programme; evaluate the credibility of their recapitalisation plan.
Agusto & Co. or GCR rating: Check the insurer's financial strength rating. An 'A' or above rating signals adequate capital and management quality.
Claims settlement record: Request data on group life claims settlement times and dispute rates. Best-practice insurers settle within 30–60 days of complete documentation.

Premium adequacy: If a quoted rate appears materially below market (more than 20% below the average of at least three competitive quotes), challenge the insurer's actuarial basis. A rate that is too low today becomes unpaid claims tomorrow.

Scheme administration capability: Assess the insurer's digital tools for schedule management, certificate issuance, and claims tracking. A scheme that requires paper-based administration creates compliance risk.

Exclusion review: Review all exclusions in the proposed master policy carefully. Unusual or broad exclusions (extended suicide exclusion periods, exclusions for common occupational diseases) should be negotiated before inception.

blocks.h: This chapter has examined group life insurance in Nigeria — its legislative mandate, its actuarial structure, its administrative mechanics, and its claims framework. The following are the chapter's essential propositions.

items.h: Group life insurance is a single insurance contract covering a defined group of lives (typically employees of a common employer) under a master policy. It is structurally, contractually, and actuarially distinct from individual life assurance.

The mandatory employer group life obligation in Nigeria arises under Section 4(5) of the Pension Reform Act 2014: every employer with three or more employees must maintain Group Life Insurance providing a minimum death benefit of three times each employee's Annual Total Emolument (ATE = Annual Basic Salary + Annual Housing Allowance + Annual Transportation Allowance). Premium must be paid before the commencement of cover. NIIRA 2025 increases the non-compliance penalty to ₦250,000 per uninsured employee.

An employer who fails to maintain the mandatory scheme is directly liable under PRA 2014, Section 4(6), to pay the death benefit from its own funds for any employee who dies while the mandatory cover was not in place. This financial exposure is potentially several multiples of the premium cost and is the most compelling compliance argument available to practitioners.

The master policy is the single contract between the insurer and the employer. Each employee receives a certificate of participation evidencing their membership. The employee has no direct contractual relationship with the insurer; rights arise through the employer and through statute.

ATE is calculated as Annual Basic Salary + Annual Housing Allowance + Annual Transportation Allowance, multiplied by the agreed benefit multiple (minimum 3×). The sum assured must be updated at each salary review to maintain compliance with the statutory minimum.

Group underwriting assesses the group as a whole, not individual members. Most members are auto-accepted without medical evidence up to the Free Cover Limit (FCL). Above the FCL, individual medical evidence is required. The FCL is scheme-specific and agreed at inception based on group size, age profile, and industry hazard.

The group life premium rate is expressed as ₦ per ₦1,000 of total sum assured. It is determined by the group's age profile, industry classification, size, and claims experience at renewal. The statutory cap on group life commission is 9% of premium (NIIRA 2025 s.62(1)(a); the earlier NAICOM guideline was 8%).

Scheme administration requires continuous maintenance of the employee schedule: adding new joiners, removing leavers, adjusting sums assured for salary changes, and renewing the master policy annually. The renewed Group Life Insurance Certificate must be submitted to PenCom each year as evidence of employer compliance.

The PRA 2014 removed the requirement for Letters of Administration to access group life death benefits. Benefits are paid directly to the named beneficiary on production of the standard documentation. Under NIIRA 2025, all claims must be settled within 60 days; delayed settlement attracts compound interest penalties.

Optional enhancements include Group Personal Accident (the most common), Total and Permanent Disability benefit, funeral expense cover, critical illness, and spouse/dependant cover. Portability and conversion rights allow departing employees to continue life cover without fresh underwriting.

blocks.h: A single insurance contract (master policy) covering the lives of all eligible members of a defined group — typically employees of a common employer. The insurer underwrites the group as a whole, not individual members. Death benefits are payable to named beneficiaries on the death of any covered member while in active service and while the scheme is in force.
The single insurance contract issued by the insurer to the employer (the group policyholder), governing the terms of the group life scheme. Not held by individual employees.

A document issued to each covered employee confirming their membership of the group scheme, their applicable sum assured, and the claims notification procedure. Evidence of membership, not a separate contract.

The base used to calculate the minimum sum assured in a group life scheme: Annual Basic Salary + Annual Housing Allowance + Annual Transportation Allowance. Minimum sum assured = 3× ATE under the Pension Reform Act 2014.
A group life scheme in which the employer pays 100% of the premium. The PRA 2014 mandatory group life scheme is non-contributory. Supplementary cover above the minimum may be contributory.
A group life scheme (typically a supplementary layer above the mandatory minimum) in which employees contribute to or fully fund additional cover. Employee contributions are voluntary.

The maximum sum assured per employee at which the insurer accepts group scheme members automatically without individual medical evidence. Members with sum assured above the FCL must provide satisfactory health evidence for the excess.

The assessment of mortality risk based on the characteristics of the group as a whole, rather than individual medical assessment. Produces lower premiums and broader accessibility than individual underwriting.

The list of covered employees maintained by the insurer under the master policy. Must be kept current by the employer through prompt notification of new hires, salary changes, and terminations. The schedule is the definitive record for claims processing.
National Pension Commission. Supervises employer compliance with the PRA 2014 group life obligation. Receives the annual Group Life Insurance Certificate from employers as evidence of compliance.
The lump-sum payment to a covered employee's beneficiary on the employee's death while in active service under a compliant group life scheme.

A right attached to a group life policy allowing a departing employee to continue term cover with the same insurer on an individual basis, without fresh medical underwriting, by exercising the right within the prescribed window.
A right allowing a departing employee to convert their group term life cover to an individual permanent (whole life) policy without evidence of insurability, exercised within the prescribed window.
The group life premium expressed as the amount payable for every ₦1,000 of total sum assured. Total annual premium = (Total Sum Assured ÷ 1,000) × Rate per ₦1,000.

The maximum broker commission on group life assurance business, set by NAICOM in its 2011 Operational Guidelines and maintained under NIIRA 2025. Introduced to curb destructive rate competition on the Federal Government's group life scheme.
